prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "RIO TINTO PLC" (ticker RIO), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "RIO", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Rio Tinto plc (dual-listed Rio Tinto Group with Rio Tinto Limited)

mission.statement: Finding better ways to provide the materials the world needs
mission.source: Rio Tinto company website (riotinto.com), stated as the group's purpose
mission.plain: Rio Tinto wants to dig up and process the metals and minerals the world relies on in smarter, cleaner and safer ways.

about.plain: Rio Tinto digs huge amounts of rock out of the ground and turns it into raw materials. Its biggest product is iron ore from Western Australia, which steel mills melt to make steel. It also makes aluminium, mines copper and gold, and has started producing lithium for batteries. It sells these materials to factories all over the world, especially in China.
about.customers: Mostly steel mills in China and Asia, plus aluminium, copper and battery-material buyers around the world.
about.everyday: The steel in cars and buildings, the aluminium in drink cans and the copper in electric wiring can all start out as rock dug up by companies like Rio Tinto.

money.plain: rock that steel mills turn into steel
aluminium metal and the ore it comes from
copper for wires, motors and power grids

result.summary: Rio Tinto has a real but narrow advantage: its Pilbara iron ore mines, with their own railways and ports, are among the lowest-cost in the world, and it owns rare long-life deposits such as Oyu Tolgoi copper and Simandou iron ore. It sells undifferentiated commodities at market prices, so its edge is low cost and hard-to-replace assets rather than brand or customer lock-in.

pricingPower.evidence: Rio is a price-taker: iron ore revenue fell from $33,772m in 2023 to $28,376m in 2025 even though Pilbara shipments were steady (326.2 Mt in 2025 vs 328.6 Mt in 2024, 100% basis), because index prices fell; its margins move with commodity prices it does not set.

moats.evidence: Buyers choose on grade, price and reliability rather than brand; Rio's reputation was damaged by the 2020 destruction of the Juukan Gorge rock shelters.
Steel mills blend ores and have tuned furnaces to Pilbara Blend, which gives some stickiness, but they can and do switch between Rio, BHP, Vale and Fortescue ore.
Selling ore and metal does not become more valuable to one customer because others also buy it.

Its integrated Pilbara system of mines, private railways and ports shipped 326.2 Mt in 2025 and sits in the lowest part of the global cost curve; group underlying EBITDA margin was about 44% in 2025 ($25,363m on $57,638m).
The seaborne iron ore market is dominated by a few miners (Rio, BHP, Vale, Fortescue), and new rail-and-port supply chains cost tens of billions and take a decade, as Simandou shows.
Rio's business model is the same as its large diversified peers.

Decades of operating know-how such as AutoHaul driverless trains and autonomous trucks, the ELYSIS carbon-free smelting joint venture with Alcoa, and lithium direct-extraction at Rincon give some edge, though peers run similar technology.

It owns rare tier-one orebodies: the Pilbara iron ore province, Oyu Tolgoi in Mongolia (copper output up 61% in 2025), Kennecott, Simandou's high-grade (about 65% Fe) ore in Guinea, and Arcadium's lithium assets bought in 2025.

customers.evidence: Chinese steel mills have bought Pilbara ore for decades and Rio sells most ore under long-standing relationships, but purchases follow price and grade rather than loyalty, and China's state buyer China Mineral Resources Group now negotiates for mills.

talent.evidence: Rio is a large, well-paid employer in Australia, Canada and Mongolia, but its 2022 Everyday Respect report found widespread bullying and harassment, and no independent top-employer ranking was verified.

product.evidence: Its products are commodities; Pilbara Blend is a benchmark ore, Simandou adds premium high-grade ore and its hydro-powered Canadian aluminium is low-carbon, but none is clearly superior to rivals' equivalent grades.

competitors.name: BHP Group
competitors.note: Neighbouring Pilbara iron ore operations and large copper producer; Rio's closest diversified peer.

competitors.name: Vale
competitors.note: Brazilian iron ore giant competing for the same Chinese steel mill customers; also copper and nickel.

competitors.name: Fortescue
competitors.note: Pilbara iron ore producer selling to Chinese mills.

competitors.name: Glencore
competitors.note: Copper, aluminium and commodity trading; Rio held and ended merger talks with it in January to February 2026.

competitors.name: Anglo American (merging with Teck)
competitors.note: Copper in Chile and Peru and Kumba iron ore.

competitors.name: Alcoa
competitors.note: Bauxite, alumina and aluminium; also Rio's partner in the ELYSIS smelting venture.

competitors.name: China Hongqiao Group
competitors.note: World's largest private aluminium producer, also big in Guinea bauxite.

competitors.name: Freeport-McMoRan
competitors.note: Large listed copper and gold producer.

competitors.name: Codelco
competitors.note: Chilean state-owned copper producer, the largest copper miner.

competitors.name: Aluminum Corporation of China (Chalco)
competitors.note: State-backed Chinese alumina and aluminium producer; partner (via Chinalco) in Simandou.

competitors.name: Southern Copper
competitors.note: Low-cost copper mines in Peru and Mexico.

competitors.name: Albemarle
competitors.note: Largest listed lithium producer, competing with the former Arcadium assets.

competitors.name: SQM
competitors.note: Chilean lithium brine producer competing in lithium carbonate.

marketShare.measure: tonnes (Rio Tinto 2025 Pilbara shipments 326.2 Mt and BHP WAIO FY2026 production 291.2 Mt, both 100% basis / USGS 2025e world usable ore 2,600 Mt)
tonnes (Rio Tinto 2025 primary aluminium 3,380 kt / USGS 2025e world smelter production 74,000 kt)
tonnes (Rio Tinto 2025 consolidated copper 883 kt / USGS 2025 world mine production 23,000 kt; BHP uses fiscal year to June 2026)

threats: A slowdown in Chinese steel output and property construction cutting iron ore demand and prices (iron ore was 49% of 2025 revenue).
New high-grade supply from Simandou and other projects pushing iron ore prices lower, including against Rio's own Pilbara ore.
China's state iron ore buyer (China Mineral Resources Group) strengthening buyers' bargaining power.
Resource nationalism and tax disputes, e.g. Oyu Tolgoi's $443m Mongolian tax payment in H1 2026 and operating in Guinea.
Social licence and governance risk after the 2020 Juukan Gorge destruction and the 2022 workplace culture report.
Higher net debt ($14.1bn at June 2026, from $5.5bn at end-2024) after the Arcadium lithium purchase and heavy Simandou spending.
Weak lithium prices and slower ramp-ups (2026 lithium output guided to the low end of 61-64 kt).
Operational incidents such as the 2026 Kennecott smelter furnace breach and a September 2026 seismic event at a Kennecott underground mine.

ceo.name: Simon Trott
ceo.background: Grew up on a Western Australian wheatbelt farm; Bachelor of Agriculture, University of Western Australia (1998); about two decades at Rio Tinto, including first Chief Commercial Officer and Iron Ore chief executive before becoming CEO on 25 August 2025

c1.evidence: Rio leads mature, cyclical industries (seaborne iron ore, aluminium); 2025 revenue of $57,638m was below 2021's $63,495m, so it is not leading a fast-growing emerging industry.

c2.evidence: Customers buy Rio's ore mainly because it is low-cost, reliable, high-volume Pilbara Blend from a world-class rail and port system; the asset base is hard to copy but the product itself is a commodity.

c3.evidence: Rio Tinto is a famous name in mining and investing but ordinary consumers rarely know it, and BHP rather than Rio is usually called the world's biggest miner.

c4.evidence: Its purpose 'Finding better ways to provide the materials the world needs' is repeated in reports, but management is judged mainly on returns and costs, with targets such as $1.8bn of annualised productivity benefits by end-2026.

c6.evidence: “big miner, iron ore, Juukan Gorge, China-dependent” — the impression is mixed: respected as a low-cost producer but tarnished by the 2020 destruction of Aboriginal heritage sites.

c7.evidence: Its markets are huge, and copper, aluminium and lithium ride the electrification trend, but iron ore, half of revenue, depends on Chinese steel demand that may have peaked.

c8.evidence: Rio is expanding into lithium (Arcadium, bought March 2025; Rincon targeting about 200 ktpa LCE capacity by 2028) and copper growth, aiming for 3% CuEq production growth a year to 2030.

m1.evidence: Simon Trott's plan is a practical 'stronger, sharper and simpler' operating agenda focused on costs and execution rather than a bold new vision.

m2.evidence: Trott is a long-serving professional manager, not a founder; he became CEO in August 2025 after about two decades at the company.

m4.evidence: Trott emphasises 'values-based performance culture' and partnerships, but there is no independent evidence yet of a distinctly servant-style leadership.

m5.evidence: Rio runs innovation programs (AutoHaul autonomous trains, ELYSIS carbon-free smelting, lithium direct extraction), but its culture is a traditional large-miner culture still recovering from the 2022 Everyday Respect report.

m6.evidence: Trott has deep operational knowledge from running Iron Ore and Commercial, but his background is agriculture and commerce rather than engineering.

m7.evidence: Rio has made heritage, safety and decarbonisation commitments (50% Scope 1 and 2 emissions cut target by 2030), but past failures like Juukan Gorge weigh on its record.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Simon Trott at a top university was found.

m8b.evidence: Trott has a low-key, operational public profile rather than a distinctive personal brand.

m9.evidence: As Iron Ore chief he delivered stable Pilbara output, and in his first year as CEO H1 2026 underlying EBITDA rose 28% to $14,826m, but his tenure as CEO is barely a year old.

m10.evidence: Trott is driving cost cuts (2025 operating unit cost down 5%; $1.8bn productivity run-rate target), but Rio is not known for a frugal culture.

c10.evidence: Its iron ore, aluminium and copper go into steel, cars, buildings, grids and batteries used by billions, but this is indirect and rivals supply the same materials.

p2.evidence: Building and running giant mines, rail and ports such as Simandou (a new trans-Guinean railway and port) and the Oyu Tolgoi underground mine is extremely hard, and the materials are essential to the world economy.

f2.evidence: Operating margin fell from 37.7% in 2020 ($16,829m on $44,611m) to 25.9% in 2025 ($14,936m on $57,638m); Rio does not report a gross margin.

f3.evidence: Equity is positive ($67.0bn at end-2025), and net debt of $14.1bn at June 2026 is about 0.55 times 2025 underlying EBITDA, but borrowings ($21.4bn) exceed cash ($8.9bn).

f4.evidence: Operating profit fell from $16,829m in 2020 to $14,936m in 2025, while operating cash flow was roughly flat ($15,875m to $16,832m).

v1.evidence: Its ore and metals are commodities sold on index prices; there is no practical reason an ordinary buyer would pick Rio's iron ore over BHP's or Vale's of the same grade.

v2.evidence: No top employer ranking was verified, and the 2022 independent Everyday Respect review found systemic bullying, sexism and racism at the company.

c5.evidence: Its materials are vital, but if Rio disappeared, rivals and new projects would largely replace its supply over time; steel mills and aluminium users would notice higher prices in the short term.
